body.heading: Wind at the surface, density below
paragraphs: Surface currents are driven mainly by wind. The great wind belts drag the top layer of the sea along, and Earth's rotation deflects the flow until it settles into huge circular gyres in each ocean basin. The Gulf Stream, part of the Atlantic gyre, carries warm water from the tropics toward northern Europe at rates dwarfing all the world's rivers combined.

Beneath the surface, a slower global circulation runs on density: cold, salty water in the North Atlantic and around Antarctica sinks and creeps along the deep floor, while warmer water rises elsewhere. A full circuit of this 'conveyor belt' can take around a thousand years.

body.heading: Why currents matter on land
paragraphs: Currents are climate machinery. They move heat from the tropics toward the poles, softening winters in places like Britain that sit at latitudes as cold as Canada's. They also drive upwelling, where deep water rises and fertilises surface life, creating some of the richest fisheries on Earth.
Anything that drifts — turtle hatchlings, coconuts, lost cargo, spilled plastic — rides these rivers. To predict where something at sea will go, you start with the currents.

takeaway: Ocean currents are wind-driven surface gyres and a slow deep conveyor that together move heat and life around the planet.
